newsitem.title: USA: CLINTON SAYS MEDICARE REFORM POSSIBLE BY 2000.
newsitem.headline: CLINTON SAYS MEDICARE REFORM POSSIBLE BY 2000.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday Medicare reform would be possible in 1999, when a bipartisan commission releases its report on the program, despite the approach of the 2000 presidential election.

Speaking at a news conference, Clinton said he would have been happy for the commission, which is to find ways to trim the health care program for the elderly, to have issued its report next year instead of in 1999 as decided by Congress.
But he also noted that the commission, whose members have yet to be named, may make interim recommendations, permitting a quicker start on reforming the burgeoning program.
"I believe if there is strong bipartisan support, you can do it in an election year as well as in a non-election year," Clinton said.

"The commission may decide to make interim recommendations and then we may take a series of steps," he added. "If they make a package of recommendations at the end and it has the support of all these appointees ... then I think the Congress will be prepared to act on it."

Having this week signed legislation to balance the federal budget deficit by 2002, Clinton and Congress are now beginning to focus on the next threat to fiscal policy: the huge health care spending needed when the Baby Boom generation retires.

Clinton said he was confident the country would be able to grapple with the problem, which is politically sensitive because the influential U.S. elderly population is reluctant to see its Medicare health care benefits trimmed.
He said he also expects the Social Security retirement income program to be reformed, although the White House and Congress have yet to decide on a strategy for approaching this issue.

"Do I think that we will take the steps necessary to reform them? I do," Clinton said. "I'm the oldest of the Baby Boomers. I don't believe that our generation wants to ask our children to make drastic sacrifices to support us because we wouldn't take modest steps now that don't have to affect the people that are now retired at all," he added.
